blocks.content: SQL GROUP BY covered collapsing many rows into one summary row per group. SQL HAVING covers the natural next question, once you have those grouped results, how do you filter them down to only the groups that actually matter, the ones meeting some condition based on their own aggregate values.

This topic covers exactly why WHERE genuinely cannot do this job, how HAVING and WHERE combine when used together in one query, and a genuinely common confusion around when a filter actually belongs in HAVING versus when it really belongs in WHERE instead.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438310527-433953910.png
1. WHERE Filters Rows, HAVING Filters Groups
blocks.text: 1. WHERE Filters Rows, HAVING Filters Groups

blocks.content: WHERE filters individual rows, and it genuinely runs before grouping happens at all, as covered in the real SQL execution order earlier in this course. By the time WHERE actually runs, GROUP BY has not yet collapsed anything into summary rows.

HAVING filters grouped results, and it genuinely runs after GROUP BY has already computed those groups and their aggregate values. This is the fundamental, real difference between the two, not just a stylistic choice between similar sounding keywords.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438310529-898882470.png
blocks.alt: WHERE Filters Rows, HAVING Filters Groups

blocks.content: 2. Why WHERE Genuinely Cannot Filter an Aggregate
blocks.text: 2. Why WHERE Genuinely Cannot Filter an Aggregate

blocks.content: Trying to write WHERE COUNT star greater than 5 genuinely fails, since at the point WHERE actually runs, no aggregate value exists yet at all, COUNT has not been computed, because grouping has not happened yet either.

Trying HAVING COUNT star greater than 5 instead genuinely works, since by the point HAVING runs, GROUP BY has already computed the count for each group, giving HAVING a real, actual aggregate value to compare against.

3. A Worked Example
A concrete query shows HAVING applied to a real, common question. An orders table grouped by department needs to be filtered down to only the departments with a genuinely significant order volume.

SELECT department, COUNT(*)
FROM orders
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*)>10;
blocks.code:
SELECT department, COUNT(*)
FROM orders
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*)>10;

codes.sql:
SELECT department, COUNT(*)
FROM orders
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*)>10;

blocks.content: This query groups orders by department, computes each department order count, and then keeps only the departments where that count is genuinely above ten, discarding smaller departments from the final result entirely.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438310530-126643529.png

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Writing WHERE COUNT star greater than some number instead of HAVING. This is one of the single most common SQL errors beginners hit, and it traces directly back to the real execution order, WHERE simply runs too early to see any aggregate value.
4. Using WHERE and HAVING Together

A single query genuinely can, and often should, use both WHERE and HAVING together, each doing its own distinct job. WHERE filters individual rows first, before any grouping happens, removing rows that should not even be considered for grouping at all.

GROUP BY then groups whatever rows actually survived that WHERE filter. HAVING then filters those grouped results further, based on an aggregate value computed only from the rows that made it through both the WHERE filter and the grouping step.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438310530-945565462.png
5. HAVING Without an Aggregate Condition

HAVING with no genuine aggregate condition at all, just a plain comparison on a grouped column, technically works in most databases, but it is genuinely no different from writing that same condition in WHERE, and using WHERE for it is genuinely clearer and often faster.

HAVING filtering on a genuine aggregate value, a count, a sum, an average computed per group, is the actual, genuine reason HAVING exists as a separate clause at all, not a stylistic alternative to WHERE.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438310531-571225077.png

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: If a filter does not actually reference an aggregate function, it almost always belongs in WHERE, not HAVING, since WHERE runs earlier and is generally more efficient for filtering individual rows before any grouping work happens.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine HAVING usage. Using WHERE to filter an aggregate value, which genuinely fails since no aggregate exists at that point in execution. Using HAVING for a filter that genuinely belongs in WHERE, a plain, non aggregate condition, which works but is less clear and often less efficient.
And forgetting that HAVING genuinely requires GROUP BY to actually make sense, since HAVING filters groups, and without GROUP BY, there are no genuine groups for it to filter in the first place.
